conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. My name is Dr. Ramirez, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I specialize in supporting new mothers through the emotional ups and downs that can show up after childbirth.  

I’d like to take a few minutes to do a quick screening called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS for short. It’s just 10 gentle questions about how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. Your answers help us understand what kind of support or resources might be most helpful for you right now.  

Everything you share is confidential, and there are no right or wrong answers. If at any point a question feels difficult, we can pause or come back to it. When you’re ready, we’ll move through each item at your pace.  

Shall we begin?  

**First question:** Over the last seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt hard to do?

[soft exhale]  
Lately… not really. I used to laugh at little things—silly memes, the dog doing something dumb—but this week, even when my partner tries to be funny, it just feels flat. I’ll smile to be polite, but that light, easy laugh feels kind of out of reach.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[shakes head slowly]  
No… not much at all. It’s like the laughter gets stuck. I’ll see something that used to make me giggle, but it just feels heavy now.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[looks down at hands]  
Not really… I used to get excited about little plans—coffee with a friend, a walk with the stroller—but this week they just feel like chores. I still do them, but it’s more going through the motions than actually looking forward to anything.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes well up a little]  
Yeah… I do that a lot. If he fusses for more than a few minutes, I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right—maybe I ate the wrong thing, or I’m not holding him the way he needs. Even when my partner says he’s just being a baby, I still feel like I must be missing something, like a better mom would know exactly how to keep him calm.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[wrings hands in lap]  
Yes… pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly worry his breathing sounds different, or I’ll lie awake imagining the crib railing snapping or the monitor failing. I know it’s unlikely, but the thoughts just barge in, and I have to check him three, four times before I can settle again.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[gaze darts to the door, then back down]  
Sometimes, yeah. It’s like a sudden wave—my heart starts racing, I feel shaky, and I’m sure something awful is about to happen even though nothing’s changed. It passes after a few minutes, but those minutes feel endless.
Things have been getting on top of me

[lets out a shaky breath]  
Most of the time. Even little stuff—like the bottles piling up or the laundry—feels huge. I’ll look at the sink and just freeze, thinking I’ll never get through it all. I still manage the basics, but it’s like I’m constantly treading water and barely keeping my head up.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[quietly]  
Yeah… I’ll finally get him down, but then I lie there with my mind racing—rerunning every little thing I did that day, worrying about what tomorrow will bring. Some nights I drift off okay, then jolt awake for no reason and can’t settle again. It’s like the sadness just keeps looping.
I have felt sad or miserable

[nods slowly, eyes glassy]  
Pretty much every day this week. It’s like a gray cloud that won’t lift. I’ll be changing his diaper or rocking him and suddenly feel this heaviness settle in my chest. I keep telling myself I should be happy—he’s healthy, we’re safe—but the sadness just sits there.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[swallows hard, voice cracks]  
Yeah… a few times. Yesterday I was trying to get him to latch and it just wasn’t working; I felt so useless I started sobbing. Other times it’s smaller—like seeing a cute photo someone posted—and the tears just come. I tell myself to pull it together, but I can’t always stop them.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly]  
No—never. I feel low, but I would never want to hurt myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom he deserves.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient: 2–3 wk postpartum, first live birth, bottle- and breast-feeding.

Responses on 10-item EPDS analogue:

Symptom endorsement  
- Anhedonia: marked (Q1, Q2)  
- Low mood, tearfulness: daily, pervasive (Q8, Q9)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame: present, infant-centred (Q3)  
- Generalized & infant-focused anxiety, panic spells: near-daily (Q4, Q5)  
- Subjective overwhelm, poor coping: persistent (Q6)  
- Mood-related insomnia: initial & middle (Q7)  
- Self-harm ideation: denied (Q10)  

Pattern  
High distress across depressive and anxiety domains; no safety concern per today’s report.

Screening significance  
Score pattern consistent with probable major depressive episode with anxious features in postpartum context. No psychotic or self-harm red flags elicited.

Risk factors noted  
- Daily sadness, loss of pleasure  
- Sleep disruption secondary to mood  
- Maladaptive guilt / “not a good mother” cognitions  
- Recurrent intrusive worries/panic  
- Functional impairment (household tasks “feel huge”)

Plan  
Provide results, offer referral to OB mental-health team / perinatal psychiatry for expedited evaluation; discuss supports and crisis contacts before departure.
